core: George Washington's presidency (first inaugurated 1789) and the precedents he set: a functioning cabinet, the two-term tradition (declining a third term in the Farewell Address, 1796), and a policy of neutrality (declared neutral in 1793)

Alexander Hamilton's financial system as Treasury secretary: the Report on Public Credit (January 1790) proposing federal assumption of state debts and funding the national debt at face value; the Report on a National Bank (December 1790) and the Bank of the United States (chartered 1791); tariffs to promote manufacturing

The rise of the first party system despite the founders' hopes: Hamilton's Federalists (strong central government, commerce, loose construction) versus Jefferson and Madison's Democratic-Republicans (agrarian, states' rights, strict construction)
The Louisiana Purchase (1803): the United States bought the Louisiana territory from France for $15 million under President Jefferson, roughly doubling the size of the country
Marbury v. Madison (1803): the Marshall Court established judicial review, the power of courts to declare acts of Congress or the executive unconstitutional
The War of 1812 (1812-1815) with Britain, ended by the Treaty of Ghent (signed December 24, 1814) restoring the prewar status quo

The Missouri Compromise (1820): Missouri admitted as a slave state and Maine as a free state, with slavery prohibited in the remaining Louisiana territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes latitude, temporarily managing sectional tension over slavery
supporting: The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 tested and demonstrated the new federal government's authority to enforce its taxes
Jefferson's constitutional doubts about acquiring territory, set aside for the Louisiana Purchase, illustrate the strict-vs-loose construction debate in practice
The Treaty of Ghent settled few of the stated causes of the War of 1812, returning boundaries to status quo ante bellum

claims.claim: George Washington, first inaugurated in 1789, built the first cabinet (Hamilton at Treasury, Jefferson at State, Knox at War, Randolph as attorney general), establishing the practice of an executive advised by department heads.

In his Farewell Address of 1796, Washington declined to seek a third term (establishing the two-term tradition), advised the nation to steer clear of permanent alliances with foreign nations, and warned against the baneful effects of the spirit of party.
Washington declared the United States neutral in 1793 amid war between Britain and revolutionary France, a policy that itself deepened the divide between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans.

As Treasury secretary, Hamilton's Report on Public Credit (January 1790) urged the federal government to assume the states' war debts and fund the national debt at face value; his Report on a National Bank (December 1790) led to the Bank of the United States, whose charter Washington signed in 1791.

Opposition to Hamilton's program led by Jefferson and Madison produced the first party system: Hamilton's Federalists favored a strong central government and commerce, while the Democratic-Republicans favored agrarian interests and states' rights.
The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 saw western Pennsylvanians protest a federal excise tax, and Washington led troops to suppress it, demonstrating the government's power to enforce its laws.

In 1803 the United States purchased the Louisiana territory from France for $15 million; the acquisition roughly doubled the size of the country. The purchase treaty was signed April 30, 1803, under President Jefferson.
Jefferson, ordinarily a strict interpreter of the Constitution, set aside doubts about whether the federal government could acquire new territory in order to complete the Louisiana Purchase.

In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review, the courts' power to determine the constitutionality of acts of the other branches; it was the first time the Supreme Court held an act of Congress unconstitutional.

The War of 1812 (1812-1815) was fought between the United States and Great Britain over impressment of American sailors, interference with neutral commerce, and frontier tensions; it ended with the Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, which restored the prewar boundaries (status quo ante bellum).

The Missouri Compromise, approved March 6, 1820, admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state to keep the sectional balance, and prohibited slavery in the remaining Louisiana territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes north latitude.

The Missouri Compromise only temporarily managed sectional tension over slavery; its 36 degrees 30 minutes line was repealed by the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 and the compromise was held unconstitutional in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Louisiana Purchase literally 'doubled' the size of the United States.
positions: Popular and government summaries state it doubled the nation's size
The exact ratio depends on how the loosely defined territory and existing U.S. area are measured
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both the National Archives ('the United States doubled its size') and OpenStax state the purchase doubled the country's size; the lesson uses 'roughly doubled' to reflect that the territory's boundaries were only loosely defined at the time.

sourceRecords.notes: Confirms Washington's cabinet (Hamilton Treasury, Jefferson State, Knox War, Randolph attorney general); Hamilton's Report on Public Credit (January 1790, assumption of state debts, funding at face value); Report on a National Bank (December 1790) and the Bank of the United States created by legislation Washington signed in 1791; tariffs; the Federalist vs Democratic-Republican split; and the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794. Original prose synthesized; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 8.2 The New American Republic
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms 'Washington declared the United States neutral in 1793' amid war between Britain and revolutionary France, and that neutrality sharpened the Federalist / Democratic-Republican divide.

sourceRecords.title: U.S. History, 8.3 Partisan Politics
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms that in 1803 the United States bought Louisiana from France for $15 million and 'doubled in size,' and that in Marbury v. Madison (1803) Chief Justice John Marshall established 'the principle of judicial review' to review and possibly nullify acts of Congress and the president.

sourceRecords.title: Milestones: Louisiana Purchase and Lewis and Clark Expedition, 1803-1804
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Louisiana Purchase of 1803: $15 million paid to France under President Thomas Jefferson for roughly 828,000 square miles between the Mississippi and the Rocky Mountains, covering all or part of fifteen modern states. Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty (1803) — Milestone Documents
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the treaty was signed April 30, 1803; that with it 'the United States doubled its size'; the $15 million price for 828,000 square miles; and that Jefferson, normally a strict constructionist, set aside doubts about acquiring territory. Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Marbury v. Madison (1803) — Milestone Documents
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms Marbury v. Madison was decided in 1803; that Chief Justice John Marshall delivered the opinion establishing judicial review — 'the right of the courts to determine the constitutionality of the actions of the other two branches of government' — and that it was the first time the Court declared an act of Congress unconstitutional ('A Law repugnant to the Constitution is void'). Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Missouri Compromise (1820) — Milestone Documents
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the Missouri Compromise was approved March 6, 1820; admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state to keep the balance; prohibited slavery in the Louisiana territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes latitude; that this line held 34 years until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854; and that the compromise was ruled unconstitutional in Dred Scott (1857). Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Milestones: The War of 1812-1815
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms the War of 1812 (1812-1815) between the United States and Great Britain; causes including impressment of American seamen, searches of merchant ships, and blockades of neutral commerce; and that on Christmas Eve (December 24, 1814) negotiators signed the Treaty of Ghent, restoring boundaries to the status quo ante bellum with no clear victor. Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Milestones: Washington's Farewell Address, 1796
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms that in the Farewell Address (1796) Washington announced he would not seek a third term and cautioned the nation to avoid permanent alliances with foreign nations, relying instead on temporary alliances for emergencies. Federal government work, public domain.

sourceRecords.title: Washington's Farewell Address 1796 (full text)
sourceRecords.provider: The Avalon Project, Yale Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Public-domain primary text. Confirms Washington's warning about 'the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally' and his counsel that 'it is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.' Used to verify the two direct phrases; prose otherwise original.
